title: Intermittent Suction of the Tracheobronchial Tree
path: Intermittent Suction of the Tracheobronchial Tree

headings.title: Introduction and Purpose of Tracheobronchial Suctioning
headings.content: Intermittent suctioning of the tracheobronchial tree is a vital nursing procedure designed to maintain a patent airway, remove accumulated pulmonary secretions, and improve gas exchange in patients who are unable to clear their own airway effectively. In clinical practice, particularly within acute and critical care settings in Nigeria, patients with artificial airways such as endotracheal or tracheostomy tubes frequently develop thick or excessive mucus plugs that can lead to airway obstruction, atelectasis, and severe hypoxia. The primary purpose of intermittent suctioning is to clear these secretions mechanically while minimizing trauma to the delicate tracheal mucosa. Unlike continuous suctioning, which can cause severe mucosal damage, hypoxia, and atelectasis by constantly applying negative pressure, intermittent suctioning involves applying negative pressure only during the withdrawal of the catheter and for a limited duration. As nursing students, understanding the physiological rationale behind this technique is essential for safeguarding patient safety and optimizing respiratory outcomes. By maintaining a clear airway through proper suctioning protocols, nurses prevent respiratory infections, reduce the work of breathing, and ensure adequate oxygen delivery to vital organs.

headings.title: Indications and Contraindications for Intermittent Suction
headings.content: Recognizing the appropriate clinical situations for tracheobronchial suctioning is a core competency for nursing students. Indications for the procedure include visible or audible secretions in the artificial airway, coughing or respiratory distress, suspected aspiration of gastric or upper airway secretions, deteriorating oxygen saturation levels (SpO2), and the need to obtain a sterile sputum specimen for laboratory analysis. On the other hand, nurses must be acutely aware of contraindications and relative risks. While suctioning is often an emergency lifesaving procedure, certain conditions require extreme caution or consultation with a physician before proceeding. Contraindications include severe bronchospasm, known or suspected tracheal surgery, bleeding disorders, untreated systemic or pulmonary hypertension, and acute facial or laryngeal trauma where airway instability is a major concern. Furthermore, patients with cardiac arrhythmias or severe hypoxemia may experience life-threatening complications if suctioning is performed without adequate pre-oxygenation. Clinical judgment must guide the nurse to weigh the necessity of airway clearance against the potential adverse physiological impacts, ensuring that the procedure is performed safely and only when genuinely indicated.

headings.title: Required Equipment and Preparation
headings.content: Proper preparation of equipment and the environment ensures a smooth, aseptic procedure that protects both the patient and the healthcare provider. Essential equipment includes a functioning suction machine and regulator, a collection canister, connecting tubing, a sterile suction catheter of the correct size (typically no greater than half the internal diameter of the artificial airway to prevent severe hypoxia), sterile gloves, a sterile basin or container, sterile normal saline or water for rinsing, personal protective equipment (mask, eye protection, or face shield and gown due to the high risk of splashing secretions), and a manual resuscitation bag (Ambu bag) attached to an oxygen source. Before beginning, the nurse must verify that the suction pressure is set within safe limits—usually between 80 to 120 mmHg for adults, and lower for pediatric or neonatal patients to avoid mucosal stripping and hemorrhage. The sterile field must be established carefully, ensuring that the dominant hand remains completely sterile to handle the catheter, while the non-dominant hand controls the suction source. Having all supplies organized at the bedside before opening the sterile kit prevents delays during the procedure when the patient may be vulnerable and experiencing respiratory distress.

headings.title: Pre-Assessment and Patient Preparation
headings.content: Before initiating suctioning, thorough pre-assessment and patient preparation are mandatory to minimize complications such as severe hypoxemia, cardiac dysrhythmias, and patient anxiety. The nurse must auscultate the patient's chest sounds to establish a baseline and determine the presence of coarse crackles, rhonchi, or diminished breath sounds indicating secretion buildup. Vital signs, including heart rate, respiratory rate, blood pressure, and oxygen saturation (SpO2), must be documented. Because suctioning removes oxygen from the lungs and can provoke hypoxemia, hyperoxygenation is a critical preparatory step. The nurse should hyperoxygenate the patient using 100% oxygen via a mechanical ventilator or manual resuscitation bag for 30 to 60 seconds as prescribed, unless contraindicated. In conscious patients, clear communication is vital: the nurse must explain the procedure, let the patient know they may experience coughing or a temporary feeling of shortness of breath, and establish a simple non-verbal communication signal (such as raising a hand) if they need the procedure stopped immediately. Positioning is also important; an alert patient should be placed in a semi-Fowler's position to ease breathing and chest expansion, while an unconscious patient should be placed in a lateral position facing the nurse to prevent aspiration.

headings.title: Step-by-Step Procedure for Intermittent Suctioning
headings.content: Executing the step-by-step procedure requires strict adherence to aseptic technique and time limits. First, don personal protective equipment and establish a sterile field. Using sterile gloves, connect the sterile suction catheter to the connecting tubing held by the non-dominant hand. Without applying suction, gently and swiftly insert the catheter through the artificial airway until resistance is met at the carina, or until the patient coughs, then withdraw it approximately 1 to 2 centimeters to avoid mucosal damage. Apply intermittent suction by placing and releasing your thumb over the control port while withdrawing the catheter in a continuous, rotating motion. The entire suctioning pass, from insertion to withdrawal, must not exceed 10 to 15 seconds to prevent severe hypoxia and vagal stimulation. After the pass, flush the catheter with sterile normal saline to clear the lumen. Allow the patient to rest and recover, re-administering supplemental oxygen between passes if needed. Limit suction passes to a maximum of three per session. Never routinely instill normal saline into the artificial airway before suctioning unless specifically ordered, as evidence shows it can push secretions deeper, cause severe desaturation, and introduce pathogens into the lower respiratory tract.

headings.title: Potential Complications and Nursing Interventions
headings.content: Tracheobronchial suctioning is an invasive procedure associated with several potential complications that require vigilant nursing monitoring and immediate intervention. Hypoxemia is one of the most common adverse events, which can be mitigated by ensuring adequate pre-oxygenation and limiting suction duration. Cardiac arrhythmias, such as bradycardia, premature ventricular contractions, or tachycardia, may occur due to vagal nerve stimulation or severe hypoxemia; if an arrhythmia develops, the nurse must immediately stop suctioning, administer 100% oxygen, and notify the physician. Mucosal trauma, bleeding, and ulceration can result from excessive suction pressure, oversized catheters, or overly aggressive insertion; using correct pressure settings and gentle handling prevents this. Pulmonary atelectasis may be triggered by using excessive negative pressure or large catheter sizes relative to the airway. Infection, including ventilator-associated pneumonia, is another major risk; nurses must strictly adhere to universal precautions and aseptic technique throughout the procedure. Finally, bronchospasm can be provoked by the physical irritation of the catheter; bronchodilator therapy may be required if severe wheezing occurs.

headings.title: Post-Procedure Evaluation and Documentation
headings.content: The nursing process concludes with comprehensive post-procedure evaluation and meticulous documentation. Immediately following suctioning, the nurse must re-evaluate the patient's respiratory status by auscultating lung sounds to determine if secretions have been successfully cleared and breath sounds have improved. Vital signs, including heart rate, respiratory rate, and oxygen saturation, must be checked and compared against pre-procedure baselines to ensure the patient has recovered well without prolonged desaturation or distress. The nurse should observe the patient's overall comfort level, skin color, and work of breathing. Finally, accurate documentation in the patient's clinical record is legally and professionally mandatory. The nursing note must include the date and time of the procedure, the indication for suctioning, the patient's pre- and post-procedure vital signs and breath sounds, the size of the catheter used, the amount, color, consistency, and odor of the secretions obtained, how well the patient tolerated the procedure, and any complications encountered along with the nursing interventions taken. Proper documentation ensures continuity of care and provides an objective record of the patient's respiratory progress.
